articles.title: The Year-Round Home Maintenance Checklist
articles.subtitle: Season-by-Season Guide for Homeowners
articles.metaDescription: A season-by-season home maintenance checklist — spring, summer, fall, and winter — plus how often to do each task and when to hire a pro. Free to use.
articles.ctaTitle: Get your home's to-do list done
articles.ctaBody: Describe what needs doing and TradeWorks helps you browse, choose, and book a vetted, insured pro. Membership is free, you pay the pro directly with no markup, and you earn a small percentage back in service credits.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Year-round home maintenance is a season-by-season routine — spring, summer, fall, and winter — that keeps your home's systems running and stops small problems from turning into expensive repairs. A good rule of thumb is to budget roughly 1% of your home's value each year for upkeep. Most tasks on this list are simple enough to do yourself; a few — HVAC, roofing, chimney, and electrical work — are worth handing to a vetted pro.

sections.heading: Why year-round maintenance pays off
paragraphs: Homes fail on a schedule. Filters clog, seals dry out, gutters fill with debris, and small leaks spread quietly until something gives way at the worst possible moment. Spreading a little upkeep across the year is the cheapest insurance you can buy: it protects your most expensive systems, keeps energy bills in check, and preserves the value of the home itself.

The 1% rule is a helpful anchor. On a $400,000 home, that's about $4,000 a year set aside for maintenance and repairs. In practice, many years cost far less — and the routine work below is exactly what keeps the occasional big-ticket repair from arriving early. Think of each task as buying time on a system you'd rather not replace before you have to.

The checklists that follow are organized by season, then summarized by frequency and by system so you can plan the way that suits you best. After any major storm, add an extra roof and exterior check regardless of the time of year.

sections.heading: The real cost of skipping maintenance
paragraphs: Deferred maintenance rarely stays the same size. A dripping supply line behind a cabinet is a cheap part when you catch it; left alone, it warps the cabinet, feeds mold, and becomes a subfloor repair that runs into the thousands. Gutters that overflow for a season send water down the fascia and against the foundation — which is how a routine cleaning turns into a drainage or grading project. A furnace that never gets serviced works harder, fails sooner, and tends to quit on the coldest night of the year, when emergency rates apply.

The pattern is always the same: small, boring, and cheap on your schedule, or large, urgent, and expensive on the system's schedule instead. Routine upkeep is really a bet that a little attention now beats a big bill later, and it's a bet that almost always pays.

There's an efficiency dividend, too. A clean filter and a tuned system move air with less energy, sealed gaps and adequate insulation keep conditioned air inside, and a flushed water heater runs more efficiently. The same tasks that prevent breakdowns quietly trim your monthly bills, which means good maintenance often pays for part of itself long before anything breaks.

sections.heading: Spring home maintenance checklist
paragraphs: Spring is for undoing winter and getting ahead of summer heat. Start outside, where the weather did the most damage, then move indoors to the systems you'll lean on when it warms up. The single highest-value job this season is getting the air conditioner serviced before the first heat wave — it's the difference between a routine tune-up and an emergency call in July.
Inspect the roof for shingles lifted or lost over winter, and check flashing around vents and chimneys.
Clean gutters and downspouts so spring rain drains away from the foundation.
Service the air conditioner before the first hot stretch — a tune-up now prevents a mid-summer breakdown.
Check outdoor faucets and sprinkler heads for freeze damage, and test the irrigation system.
Reseal the deck and look over siding, trim, and exterior paint for peeling or rot.
Test every smoke and carbon-monoxide detector and replace batteries.
Hire a vetted pro for: AC tune-up · roof inspection · gutter cleaning

sections.heading: Summer home maintenance checklist
paragraphs: Summer maintenance is about keeping cooling costs down, staying ahead of pests, and tackling the outdoor projects that need dry, warm weather. With the AC running hard, filters and airflow matter most now; outside, it's the season to wash, trim, and seal before heat and humidity do their worst.
Replace HVAC filters monthly during heavy-use months to protect the system and your air quality.
Pressure wash the driveway, walkways, and siding to clear built-up grime and mildew.
Trim trees and shrubs back from the house, the roof, and the AC unit.
Check under sinks and around appliances for slow plumbing leaks.
Test GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths, and outdoor areas.
Seal gaps and cracks around the foundation and entry points to keep pests out.
Hire a vetted pro for: pressure washing · tree trimming · pest control

sections.heading: Fall home maintenance checklist
paragraphs: Fall is the most important season for prevention, because everything you do now pays off when the weather turns. The goal is simple: get the home sealed, the heating serviced and ready, and water routed away from the house before the first freeze arrives.
Service the furnace or heating system so it's ready before you need it.
Clean the gutters again once the leaves have dropped.
Winterize outdoor faucets and blow out or drain the sprinkler system.
Have the chimney inspected and swept before the first fire — creosote buildup is a real fire and carbon-monoxide risk.
Check weatherstripping and insulation, and reverse ceiling fans to push warm air down.
Re-test detectors and refresh batteries heading into the heating season.
Hire a vetted pro for: furnace service · chimney inspection · insulation

sections.heading: Winter home maintenance checklist
paragraphs: Winter maintenance is mostly about protection — keeping pipes from freezing, water out of the house, and the heating system running efficiently. The tasks are lighter than fall's, but the stakes are high: a single frozen pipe or a failed sump pump during a storm can cause more damage in an hour than a year of upkeep costs.
Protect exposed pipes in unheated spaces and know where your main shut-off is.
Keep gutters clear and watch the roofline for ice dams after snow.
Change HVAC filters and monitor indoor humidity to protect wood and comfort.
Test the sump pump before heavy winter rains.
Check the attic for insulation gaps and signs of moisture.
Seal drafts around windows and doors to cut heating costs.
Hire a vetted pro for: plumbing / freeze protection · insulation

sections.heading: Maintenance frequency at a glance
paragraphs: If seasons aren't how your brain works, here's the same routine organized by how often each task comes up. Use it as a running checklist through the year.

sections.heading: Monthly
paragraphs: Replace the HVAC filter · test smoke and CO detectors · clean the range hood and garbage disposal · scan under sinks for leaks

sections.heading: Quarterly
paragraphs: Test GFCI outlets · run water in unused drains and traps · check caulking and grout · inspect the water-heater area

sections.heading: Twice a year
paragraphs: AC and heating service · gutter cleaning · replace detector batteries · flush the water heater

sections.heading: Annually
paragraphs: Roof inspection · chimney sweep · dryer-vent cleaning · pressure washing · sprinkler check · pest inspection

sections.heading: After a storm
paragraphs: Extra roof and exterior check — look for lifted shingles, debris damage, and drainage problems

sections.heading: Maintenance by system, and how long each one lasts
paragraphs: Knowing a system's lifespan helps you plan — and tells you when maintenance is buying time versus when it's time to budget for a replacement. These ranges are typical and vary with use, climate, and product quality.

sections.heading: Filter monthly; professional service twice a year
Inspect yearly and after storms; keep gutters clear
Flush yearly; watch for corrosion and moisture
Wash yearly; reseal the deck every 2–3 years
Check for leaks; know the main shut-off
Fixtures vary widely
paragraphs: Reading that table top to bottom is a quick way to see where you are on each system's clock. A twelve-year-old water heater that still works owes you nothing — but it's the right moment to budget for its replacement rather than be surprised by a cold shower and a flooded closet. An HVAC system past fifteen years is a candidate for a repair-or-replace conversation the next time it needs a major part.

sections.heading: Budgeting: maintenance vs. repairs
paragraphs: It helps to separate two buckets. Maintenance is the predictable, recurring spend — filters, service visits, cleanings — that you can plan almost to the dollar. Repairs and replacements are the lumpy, occasional costs that arrive on no fixed schedule. The 1% rule covers both, but the smartest approach is to treat it like a sinking fund: set aside a little each month so the money is already there when the water heater or the roof finally has its day.

If 1% sounds like a lot, remember it's an average across the life of the home, not a bill every year. Newer homes and recently updated systems often cost far less to keep up; older homes and original systems trend higher. Track what you actually spend for a couple of years and you'll have a budget tuned to your specific house — and a much clearer picture of when maintenance is winning and when it's time to replace.
What you can do yourself vs. when to call a pro

Plenty of maintenance is genuinely DIY — a filter, a detector battery, a bead of caulk. The line to respect is height, gas, and electricity: those jobs carry real risk and usually a warranty worth protecting. Here's a simple split.

sections.heading: Changing HVAC filters and testing detectors
Cleaning single-story gutters from a stable ladder
Pressure washing and routine yard care
HVAC and furnace service and repair
paragraphs: Roof work and anything on a steep or high roof

sections.heading: Electrical panel work and gas appliances
Chimney sweeping and tree removal
paragraphs: The dividing line isn't difficulty so much as consequence. Gas and electrical work carry life-safety risk and are often regulated by permit; roof and tree work add height and equipment most homeowners shouldn't improvise; and many of these systems carry manufacturer warranties that require licensed installation to stay valid. Paying a vetted, insured pro for that short list protects you, your home, and the coverage you've already paid for.

sections.heading: Building a rhythm that sticks
paragraphs: The hardest part of home maintenance isn't any single task — it's remembering to do them at all. A simple system beats good intentions. Pick one weekend near the start of each season as your “home day” and run that season's list in an afternoon. Handle the monthly quick checks on a fixed date — the first of the month, or whenever you pay a recurring bill — so they ride along with something you already do.

Keep a short running note of what you did and when, especially service dates and any parts replaced. It turns a vague “I think we did that” into a record you can act on, makes warranty claims easier, and is genuinely useful when you sell. And if you'd rather not track it yourself, this is exactly where proactive reminders earn their keep.

sections.heading: When a task can't wait for the season
paragraphs: Some warning signs override the calendar. A burning smell from an outlet or panel, a gas odor, water spreading across a ceiling, a breaker that keeps tripping, sewage backing up, or no heat in a hard freeze aren't maintenance items — they're same-day problems. Shut off the water, gas, or power at the source if it's safe to do so, and get a licensed pro out quickly. Staying on top of the routine work on this list makes these emergencies rarer, but when one does happen, speed matters more than budget.

When something on this list needs a pro, just say what's going on — "my gutters are overflowing" — and TradeWorks' AI intake assistant points you to the right service and the vetted, insured pros who cover your area.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Maintenance is seasonal — spring, summer, fall, and winter, plus monthly quick checks.
Budget about 1% of your home's value a year for upkeep and repairs.
Most tasks are DIY; hire a vetted pro for HVAC, roof, electrical, gas, and chimney work.
Inspect the roof yearly and after storms; clean gutters twice a year.
With TradeWorks, describe the task and book a vetted pro — with reminders so nothing slips.

faqs.question: How much should I budget for home maintenance?
faqs.answer: A common rule is about 1% of your home's value each year. A $400,000 home would budget roughly $4,000 annually — some years you'll spend less, and a big repair year will spend more.

faqs.question: What home maintenance should I do every month?
faqs.answer: Replace or check the HVAC filter, test smoke and carbon-monoxide detectors, run the garbage disposal and clean the range hood, and scan under sinks for leaks.

faqs.question: What are the most important seasonal tasks?
faqs.answer: Service the AC in spring and the heating system in fall, clean gutters twice a year, inspect the roof annually, and protect pipes before the first freeze.

faqs.question: Which tasks should I always hire a pro for?
faqs.answer: HVAC service, roof work, electrical panel work, gas appliances, chimney sweeping, and tree removal — anything involving heights, gas, or electricity is worth a vetted pro.

faqs.question: How often should the roof be inspected?
faqs.answer: At least once a year, plus after any major storm. Catching a lifted shingle early is far cheaper than repairing water damage later.

faqs.question: Does maintenance really save money?
faqs.answer: Yes — routine upkeep protects big-ticket systems, keeps energy bills down, and prevents small issues from turning into major repairs, which is where the real cost lives.

faqs.question: What's the easiest way to keep up with it all?
faqs.answer: Use a season-by-season checklist and set reminders. With TradeWorks you can describe any task in plain language, book a vetted pro, and get proactive reminders when seasonal work is due.

articles.subtitle: A Homeowner's Step-by-Step Guide to Hiring with Confidence
articles.metaDescription: Learn how to vet a contractor before you hire: verify license and insurance, check reviews and references, compare quotes, spot red flags, and sign a solid contract.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: To vet a contractor, verify their license and insurance, check reviews and references, get at least three written and itemized quotes, ask the right questions, and watch for red flags like demands for large cash deposits or the absence of a written contract. Then put the full scope, price, payment schedule, timeline, and warranty in writing before any work begins. A few minutes of checks up front is the cheapest protection you'll ever buy.

sections.heading: Why vetting a contractor matters
paragraphs: Hiring the wrong contractor is one of the most expensive mistakes a homeowner can make — and one of the hardest to undo. Unlicensed or uninsured work can fail inspection, void your homeowner's insurance, and leave you personally liable if someone is injured on your property. Poor workmanship can cost more to tear out and redo than the original job, and chasing an unresponsive contractor to finish or fix their work can drag on for months.

Vetting isn't about distrust; it's about matching the size of the check you're about to write with a proportional amount of diligence. The good news is that the process is straightforward and mostly free. The steps below take a first-time hire from a name on a business card to a professional you can trust with your home — and they're the same standards a quality marketplace applies before a contractor is ever allowed to take a job.

Consider what's at stake on a typical project. A mid-size renovation can run tens of thousands of dollars, often paid in installments as the work proceeds. If the contractor disappears halfway through, does substandard work that fails inspection, or isn't insured when a worker is hurt, you can be left paying twice — once for the original job and again to fix or finish it. A little diligence up front is what keeps a big project from becoming a bigger problem.

sections.heading: The 7-step vetting checklist
paragraphs: Work through these in order. If a contractor fails an early step — no license, no proof of insurance — you can stop there and save yourself the rest.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Verify the license
paragraphs: Look the contractor up on your state's licensing board using their license number or business name. Confirm the license is active, is in the right trade for your job, and matches the name on the bid. For any work that requires a permit — electrical, plumbing, structural, roofing — an unlicensed contractor is a non-starter, no matter how good the price looks.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Confirm insurance
paragraphs: A professional carries general liability and, if they have employees, workers' compensation. Ask for a Certificate of Insurance (COI) and confirm the coverage is current; for larger jobs, ask to be named as an additional insured. Without workers' comp, an injury on your property can become your financial problem, so treat missing or expired coverage as a hard stop.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Check reviews across platforms
paragraphs: Read reviews on more than one site and look past the star average. Focus on patterns — the same complaint appearing repeatedly matters more than any single review — and on how the contractor responds to criticism. Recent reviews tell you how the business runs today, not how it ran five years ago.

sections.heading: Step 4 — Ask for references and recent work
paragraphs: Ask for two or three recent customers and actually call them. Ask whether the job finished on time and on budget, how communication was, how problems were handled, and whether they'd hire the contractor again. Photos of similar completed work — or a drive past a recent job — turn claims into evidence.

sections.heading: Step 5 — Get multiple written, itemized quotes
paragraphs: Collect at least three written estimates that break out labor, materials, and scope, not just a single bottom-line number. Comparing itemized quotes shows you what each contractor actually plans to do. Be cautious with a bid that comes in far below the others — it usually signals missing scope, cheaper materials, or a plan to raise the price later.

sections.heading: Step 6 — Ask the right questions
paragraphs: Find out who actually does the work (employees or subcontractors), who pulls the permits, what the timeline is, how payment is structured, what the warranty covers, and how cleanup is handled. Clear, confident answers are a good sign; vague or evasive ones are not.

sections.heading: Step 7 — Read the contract before you sign
paragraphs: Everything you've agreed to should be in writing: scope of work, materials, total price, payment schedule, start and finish dates, the change-order process, warranty terms, and who is responsible for permits and lien waivers. Never pay the full amount upfront, and never sign a contract with blanks in it.
At a glance. Use this as a quick checklist while you compare contractors.

sections.heading: Active, correct trade, matches the bid
Red flags to watch for
paragraphs: Any one of these is a reason to slow down; two or more is usually a reason to walk away.
Demands a large cash deposit or full payment upfront — or only accepts cash
Has no written contract — or won't provide an itemized estimate
Can't or won't provide a license number or a Certificate of Insurance

sections.heading: Uses high-pressure or “today-only” pricing tactics
paragraphs: Shows up door-to-door after a storm — be especially cautious with insurance-claim “assistance”

sections.heading: Has no verifiable physical address or online presence
Submits a bid dramatically lower than everyone else
paragraphs: Asks you to pull the permits in your own name — a sign they may not be licensed

sections.heading: Green flags: what a good contractor looks like
paragraphs: Just as useful as the warning signs are the markers of a professional you can trust:
Provides an active license and a current COI without hesitation
Gives you a written, itemized estimate and a clear contract

sections.heading: Offers verifiable references and can show similar completed work
Communicates clearly and sets a realistic timeline
paragraphs: Proposes a reasonable payment schedule tied to milestones, not a large upfront lump sum

sections.heading: Puts the workmanship warranty in writing
Questions to ask before you hire
Bring this short list to every estimate:
paragraphs: Are you licensed for this type of work, and can I have your license number?
Are you insured, and can you provide a Certificate of Insurance?
Will your own employees do the work, or subcontractors?
Who pulls the permits, and are they included in the price?
Can you provide two or three recent references?
What's the timeline, and what could delay it?
How is payment structured, and what deposit do you require?
What does your warranty cover, and for how long?
How do you handle changes or unexpected problems once work starts?
Who cleans up and hauls away debris when the job is done?

sections.heading: Understanding quotes and contracts
paragraphs: An itemized quote should spell out the scope of work, the materials and quantities, the labor, and the total — clearly enough that you can compare it line-by-line against another bid. If two quotes are thousands of dollars apart, the itemization usually explains why: a different material grade, a different scope, or work one contractor left out.

For payment, a healthy structure ties money to progress: a reasonable deposit to start, one or more progress payments as milestones are hit, and the final payment only when the work is complete and you're satisfied. Be wary of anyone who wants the whole amount before they begin. The contract should also define the change-order process in writing, so any addition to the scope comes with a written price you approve before the work happens — not a surprise on the final invoice. On larger jobs that involve subcontractors or suppliers, ask for lien waivers as you pay, so you aren't left exposed if the contractor fails to pay someone further down the chain.

Finally, understand the warranty. A workmanship warranty covers the contractor's labor for a defined period; it's separate from any manufacturer's warranty on the materials or equipment installed. Get both in writing, and confirm who to call if something goes wrong after the job is done.

sections.heading: A special note on storms and disasters
paragraphs: Be extra careful in the days after a major storm. Damage brings out legitimate, busy contractors — and also out-of-town “storm chasers” who go door to door, pressure homeowners to sign on the spot, and sometimes ask you to sign over your insurance claim before the work is even scoped. Slow the process down. Verify the license and insurance exactly as you would for any other job, get the full scope and price in writing, and never hand over an insurance claim or a large deposit to someone who showed up uninvited. If a deal supposedly has to happen “right now,” that urgency is itself the red flag.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Verify license and insurance first — if either is missing, stop there.
Check reviews and call references; look for patterns, not just star ratings.
Get at least three written, itemized quotes and compare scope, not just price.
Watch for red flags: upfront-cash demands, no contract, storm-chasers, lowball bids.

faqs.question: How do I check if a contractor is licensed?
faqs.answer: Look them up on your state's licensing board using their license number or business name. Confirm the license is active, in the right trade, and matches the name on the bid. Most states offer a free online lookup.

faqs.question: Should a contractor be bonded and insured?
faqs.answer: Yes. At minimum a contractor should carry general liability insurance, plus workers' compensation if they have employees. Bonding adds another layer of protection. Ask for a Certificate of Insurance and confirm it's current before work begins.

faqs.question: How many quotes should I get?
faqs.answer: At least three. Multiple written, itemized quotes let you compare scope and materials rather than just the bottom-line price, and they help you spot a bid that's unrealistically high or low.

faqs.question: Is it normal to pay a contractor a deposit?
faqs.answer: A reasonable deposit is normal for many jobs, but you should never pay the full amount upfront. A healthy payment schedule ties money to progress, with the final payment due only when the work is complete and you're satisfied.

faqs.question: What are the biggest red flags when hiring a contractor?
faqs.answer: Demands for large cash deposits or full payment upfront, no written contract, refusal to provide a license number or proof of insurance, high-pressure sales tactics, door-to-door solicitation after a storm, and bids far below every other quote.

faqs.question: How do I check a contractor's reviews and references?
faqs.answer: Read reviews on more than one platform and look for patterns and recent feedback rather than the star average alone. Then ask for two or three recent references and call them to ask about timeline, budget, communication, and whether they'd hire the contractor again.

articles.title: Red Flags When Hiring a Home Service Pro
articles.subtitle: The Warning Signs to Watch for at Every Stage — and What to Do
articles.primaryKeyword: red flags when hiring a contractor
articles.metaDescription: The biggest red flags when hiring a home service pro — from the first call to the final invoice — plus common scams and exactly what to do when you spot one.
articles.ctaTitle: No red flags. Just vetted pros.
articles.ctaBody: Every pro on TradeWorks is background-checked, insured, and performance-scored, with upfront pricing before you book. Describe your job, browse vetted pros, and book the one you choose. Membership is free, you pay the pro directly with no markup, and you earn service credits.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: The biggest red flags when hiring a home service pro are demands for a large cash payment upfront, no license or proof of insurance, no written contract, high-pressure or door-to-door sales tactics, and a bid far below every other quote. Any single one of these is a reason to pause and ask questions; two or more together are usually a reason to walk away and find someone else.

sections.heading: Why watching for red flags matters
paragraphs: Most contractors are honest professionals — but the ones who aren't can cost you a great deal of money, time, and stress, and a few are running outright scams. Red flags are the early warning signs that let you step back before you've signed a contract or handed over a deposit, which is the cheapest possible moment to walk away.

The warning signs below are organized by stage, from the first phone call to the middle of the job, because trouble tends to reveal itself at each step if you know what to look for. None of these signs requires special expertise to spot — just the willingness to slow down and treat a large purchase like the important decision it is. At the end, you'll find exactly what to do if you've already noticed one.

It helps to remember the asymmetry involved. Walking away from a contractor who turns out to be perfectly fine costs you a little time and a few more phone calls. Hiring one who turns out to be dishonest or careless can cost you thousands of dollars, weeks of your life, and the headache of tearing out and redoing the work. When the downside is that lopsided, it's worth heeding even a single clear warning sign rather than talking yourself out of it.

sections.heading: Red flags before you hire
paragraphs: The first conversation tells you a lot — often more than the estimate that follows. A professional running a real business answers basic questions about licensing and insurance without hesitation. Be cautious if a contractor:
Won't provide a license number, or can't be found on your state's licensing board
Can't or won't show proof of insurance (a current Certificate of Insurance)
Has no verifiable physical address, business footprint, or online presence

sections.heading: Has no reviews and refuses to provide references
paragraphs: Is only reachable through an unverified cell number with no company identity
What to do: Verify the license and insurance yourself before going any further. If a contractor is evasive about the basics, that evasiveness is the answer — move on.

sections.heading: Red flags in the quote and pricing
paragraphs: How a contractor prices and presents a job is one of the most reliable tells, because it is hard to fake for long. Watch for any of these:
A bid dramatically lower than everyone else's — usually a sign of missing scope, cheaper materials, or a plan to raise the price later
Cash-only, or a pushy “discount for cash” that leaves no paper trail

sections.heading: A vague, non-itemized estimate you can't compare line-by-line
Pressure to decide immediately, or “today-only” pricing
paragraphs: A demand for a large deposit or full payment before any work begins
Scare tactics that turn a routine repair into an urgent, expensive emergency
What to do: Get at least three written, itemized quotes and compare the scope, not just the bottom line. A price that seems too good to be true almost always is.

sections.heading: Red flags in the contract
paragraphs: The contract is your main protection if something goes wrong, so read it closely before you sign. It can raise alarms of its own:
No written contract at all — everything is a handshake
Blanks in the document, or “sign now, we'll fill in the details later”

sections.heading: No clearly defined scope, materials, timeline, or warranty
paragraphs: A payment schedule weighted heavily toward the start of the job
You're asked to pull the permits in your own name (often a sign the contractor isn't licensed to)
No mention of lien waivers on a large job that involves subcontractors or suppliers
What to do: Never sign a contract with blanks in it, and never agree to pay the full amount upfront. Everything you've discussed should be written down before work starts.

sections.heading: Red flags during the job
paragraphs: Some problems only appear once work is underway, when you are already committed and more reluctant to push back. That is exactly when to stay alert. Watch for:
Work beginning without a permit that the job clearly requires

sections.heading: A steady stream of change orders and surprise upcharges
Subcontractors you never approved doing the work
The contractor going unresponsive or repeatedly missing scheduled days
paragraphs: Pressure for more money before the agreed milestones are met

sections.heading: Quality concerns that get brushed off instead of addressed
paragraphs: What to do: Pause payments until the issue is resolved in writing, document everything with photos and dates, and don't approve additional money for work that hasn't been completed as agreed.

sections.heading: Common scams to know
paragraphs: Beyond individual red flags, a handful of scam patterns show up again and again across the country. Recognizing the shape of them early is the best protection you have:

Storm chasers and disaster fraud — out-of-town crews who go door to door after a storm, pressure you to sign on the spot, and sometimes ask you to sign over your insurance claim before the work is scoped.
Bait-and-switch — an unusually low bid to win the job, followed by “unexpected” costs once work has started and you're committed.
The “leftover materials” pitch — someone claims to have extra asphalt or materials from a nearby job and offers a driveway or roof at a discount — then does shoddy work or disappears.
Deposit and disappear — a large upfront deposit is collected and the contractor is never seen again.
Unlicensed, unpermitted work — a cheap job that fails inspection, has to be redone, and can void your homeowner's insurance if something goes wrong.

sections.heading: What to do if you spot a red flag
paragraphs: Catching a warning sign is only useful if you act on it, and the right move depends mostly on how far along you are. The earlier you catch it, the simpler your options — which is one more reason to watch for these signs before you sign or pay. Depending on where you are in the process:
1. If you haven't signed or paid, simply walk away. There are other qualified pros, and no single job is worth ignoring your instincts.
2. If you've paid a deposit or work has started, document everything — photos, dates, texts, and the contract — and put your concerns in writing to the contractor.
3. Stop further payments until the problem is resolved in writing, and don't approve money for work that isn't complete.

4. Report serious problems to your state licensing board or consumer-protection office, dispute fraudulent charges with your card issuer, and for scams, file a report with the appropriate authorities.
5. Before resuming, get a second opinion and a clear written scope so you know exactly what you're paying for.
A quick gut-check before you sign

Beyond any single warning sign, a few simple instincts will steer you right. If a contractor insists the decision has to happen right now, treat that manufactured urgency as the red flag itself — a legitimate professional will give you time to think. If something feels off in how they communicate, how they price, or how they answer basic questions, that feeling is usually worth more than the discount they are offering. And when in doubt, insist on a paper trail: a written scope, a written price, and a traceable payment method. Honest contractors have no problem putting things in writing; the ones who resist are telling you something important. None of this requires you to be an expert or to assume the worst of everyone — it just means letting the process, not the pressure, set the pace.

sections.heading: How to protect yourself from the start
paragraphs: The best defense against every red flag on this page is a little diligence before you hire. Verify the license and insurance, get at least three written and itemized quotes, check reviews and call references, read the contract in full, and tie payment to milestones rather than paying upfront. Our full walkthrough — how to vet a contractor before you hire — covers each of those steps in detail. Do them once at the start, and most of the warning signs above never get the chance to become your problem. Vetting up front turns hiring from a leap of faith into a routine — and it is the single highest-return hour you will spend on any project.

Membership is free, and you earn a small percentage back in service credits on what you book. In practice, the parts of hiring that create the most anxiety — is this person real, are they insured, will the price suddenly change — are settled before you ever pick up the phone.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
paragraphs: The clearest red flags: upfront cash demands, no license or insurance, no written contract, high pressure, and lowball bids.
Warning signs appear at every stage — the first call, the quote, the contract, and during the job.
Never sign a contract with blanks or pay the full amount before work begins.
Know the common scams: storm chasers, bait-and-switch, deposit-and-disappear.
If you spot a red flag, document everything, pause payment, and report serious problems.

faqs.question: What is the biggest red flag when hiring a contractor?
faqs.answer: A demand for a large cash payment upfront — especially with no written contract or proof of insurance. It leaves no paper trail and no recourse if the work is never finished.

faqs.question: Is it a red flag if a contractor asks for cash?
faqs.answer: A cash-only requirement or a pushy “discount for cash” is a warning sign. It can mean the contractor is unlicensed or uninsured and wants to avoid a record. Paying by a traceable method protects you.

faqs.question: Should I pay a contractor a large deposit upfront?
faqs.answer: No. A reasonable deposit is normal for many jobs, but you should never pay the full amount before work begins. A healthy payment schedule ties money to progress, with the final payment due only when the work is complete.

faqs.question: What should I do if a contractor asks me to pull the permit?
faqs.answer: Be cautious — asking the homeowner to pull the permit is often a sign the contractor isn't licensed to do so. A licensed professional typically handles permits for the work they perform.

faqs.question: How do I report a bad or fraudulent contractor?
faqs.answer: Report to your state licensing board or consumer-protection office, dispute fraudulent charges with your card issuer, and for scams file a report with the appropriate local or federal authorities. Document everything first.

faqs.question: Are storm-chasing contractors a scam?
faqs.answer: Not all are, but the pattern — going door to door after a storm, pressuring you to sign immediately, and asking to take over your insurance claim — is a major red flag. Verify credentials and never sign on the spot.

articles.title: The Home Emergency Playbook
articles.subtitle: What to Do First in Any Household Emergency — System by System
articles.primaryKeyword: what to do in a home emergency
articles.metaDescription: A home emergency playbook: the first steps for burst pipes, gas leaks, electrical faults, no heat, sewage backups, and more — plus which to shut off and who to call.
articles.ctaTitle: Something broke? Get a vetted pro, fast.
articles.ctaBody: Describe what's happening and TradeWorks points you to vetted, insured pros in your area with upfront pricing and real-time booking. Membership is free, you pay the pro directly with no markup, and you earn service credits.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: In a home emergency, protect people first, then stop the source — shut off the water, gas, or electricity at the main that controls the problem. Call 911 immediately for fire, a suspected gas leak, or anyone in danger. For burst pipes, electrical faults, sewage backups, or a heating failure in a hard freeze, shut off the affected system and get a licensed pro out fast. Keep this page handy — when something breaks, the first few minutes matter most.

sections.heading: What counts as a home emergency
paragraphs: A true home emergency is anything that puts your safety or health at immediate risk, or that will cause serious, fast-spreading damage if you wait. Fire, gas odors, sparking or smoking electrical, sewage in the home, a burst pipe flooding a room, or no heat during a hard freeze all belong in this category — they can't wait for a scheduled appointment.

Plenty of frustrating problems are urgent but not emergencies: a single slow drip, one dead outlet, a fridge that's warming, or an AC that's struggling on a mild day. Those deserve prompt attention, but you have time to compare pros and book properly. The dividing line is simple — if there is a risk to people, or damage is actively getting worse by the minute, treat it as an emergency and act on the steps below. When you're genuinely unsure, err on the side of caution.

sections.heading: The first four steps in any emergency
paragraphs: Almost every household emergency follows the same opening sequence. Commit these four steps to memory; the specific scenarios later in this guide simply apply them.
1. Make sure everyone is safe. If there's fire, a gas smell, or structural danger, get everyone (and pets) out of the house and call 911 from a safe distance. People come before property, always.

2. Stop the source. Shut off the water, gas, or electricity at the main that controls the problem — or the local valve or breaker for that fixture or circuit. This single step prevents most of the damage that follows.
3. Contain and document. Limit the spread — move valuables, soak up water, close a door — and photograph everything before you clean up. Those photos matter for your insurance claim.
4. Call the right pro. Once it's safe, get a licensed specialist for the system involved. Booking quickly is where a vetted network helps — more on that at the end.

sections.heading: Know your shutoffs before you need them
paragraphs: The single best thing you can do today is learn where your shutoffs are and how to operate them — in an emergency there's no time to go looking. Walk your home once and locate each of these.

sections.heading: Main water valve
paragraphs: Where the water line enters the home — near the meter, in a basement, garage, or an outside box
Turn the valve clockwise (or a quarter-turn on a lever) until it stops

sections.heading: Individual fixture valves
paragraphs: Under sinks and toilets, behind the washer, at the water heater
Turn the small valve clockwise to isolate just that fixture

sections.heading: Gas meter / main
paragraphs: At the gas meter outside, or where the line enters
Use a wrench to turn the valve a quarter-turn — only if you can do it safely on your way out

sections.heading: Main electrical panel
paragraphs: The breaker box — garage, basement, utility room, or exterior
Flip the large main breaker to OFF, or the specific circuit breaker

sections.heading: Water heater
paragraphs: Cold-water valve on top of the tank; the breaker or gas valve for power
Close the water valve; switch off the breaker or set the gas control to off
Tip: tag your main water and gas shutoffs and your panel with a label, and make sure everyone in the household knows where they are. A visitor or family member may be the one who has to act.

sections.heading: The home emergency playbook, situation by situation
paragraphs: Find your situation below. Each one starts with what it looks like, the moves to make right now, and who to call. When a scenario involves gas, live electricity, or structural danger, the safe move is to stop, get clear, and let a professional handle the repair — those risks are exactly why the work is licensed.

sections.heading: Burst pipe or major water leak
paragraphs: Water spraying from a pipe or pooling fast can ruin floors, walls, and belongings within minutes, so speed matters more than anything.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Shut off the water at the main (or the fixture's local valve) immediately.
If water is near outlets, wiring, or the panel, turn off electricity to that area first — never touch electrical with wet hands.
Open the lowest faucets to drain remaining pressure, then move valuables and soak up standing water.
Photograph the damage before you clean up.
When to call: Call a licensed plumber right away. If water has reached electrical or the ceiling is sagging, keep clear and treat it as urgent.

sections.heading: You smell gas (or the CO alarm sounds)
paragraphs: A rotten-egg odor, a hissing sound near a gas line, or a carbon-monoxide alarm is a life-safety emergency — treat it as the most serious situation in this guide.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Leave the house immediately and take everyone, including pets, with you.
Do not flip any switches, use phones or appliances inside, or light anything — a spark can ignite gas.
Leave the door open behind you; shut off the gas at the meter only if you can do it safely on the way out.
Do not go back inside for any reason until it's cleared.
When to call: From outside, call 911 and your gas utility's emergency line. Wait for them to confirm it's safe before re-entering. This is never a DIY repair.
Do not: Never search for a leak with a flame, and never attempt to repair a gas line yourself.

sections.heading: Electrical emergency — sparks, shocks, or a burning smell
paragraphs: Sparks from an outlet, a burning or fishy smell, buzzing, warm faceplates, or a breaker that keeps tripping all mean stop and cut the power.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Cut power to the affected circuit at the breaker — or the main breaker if you're unsure which one.
Unplug affected devices only if you can do so safely and dryly.
Never touch anything electrical while standing in water or with wet hands.
Keep a Class-C or ABC extinguisher nearby, never water, for an electrical fire.
When to call: Call 911 for active sparks, smoke, or flames. Otherwise call a licensed electrician.
Do not: Don't keep resetting a breaker that trips again — it's protecting you from a fault, and forcing it can start a fire.

sections.heading: No heat during a hard freeze
paragraphs: A heating failure in deep cold risks frozen, bursting pipes and — with some heat sources — carbon monoxide, so it earns emergency status.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Check the thermostat, the furnace's power switch, and the breaker before assuming the worst.
Let faucets drip and open cabinet doors under sinks to keep pipes from freezing.
Use only safe supplemental heat, and dress warmly.
If the furnace won't stay lit or you smell gas, stop and step outside.
When to call: Call an HVAC pro for the heating system. Call 911 or the gas/fire department for a gas smell or a CO alarm.
Do not: Never heat your home with a stove, oven, grill, or generator indoors — they produce deadly carbon monoxide.

sections.heading: No AC during extreme heat
paragraphs: In a heat wave, a broken air conditioner is a genuine health risk for young children, older adults, people with medical conditions, and pets.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Check the thermostat and breaker, and replace a clogged filter if that's the cause.
Close blinds against the sun, run fans, and drink plenty of water.
Move to the coolest part of the home, or somewhere air-conditioned if indoor temperatures climb dangerously.
Never leave anyone or a pet in a parked car, even briefly.
When to call: Call an HVAC pro for the system. Seek medical help for signs of heat illness — dizziness, nausea, a pounding headache, or confusion.

sections.heading: Sewage backing up through drains or toilets
paragraphs: Sewage coming up through a drain or toilet is a health hazard, not just an inconvenience, and often signals a main-line problem.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Stop running water and flushing anywhere in the house immediately.
Keep people and pets well away from the contaminated area.
Ventilate the space and avoid contact with the water.
Don't attempt to clear a main-line backup with chemicals or a rented auger.
When to call: Call a licensed plumber. If the backup is widespread, a water-damage restoration pro may also be needed to clean and disinfect safely.

sections.heading: Roof leak or storm damage
paragraphs: Water coming through a ceiling during a storm needs fast containment to limit the damage below.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Move valuables clear and place a bucket under the drip.
If the ceiling is bulging with trapped water, a small relief hole poked over the bucket can prevent a larger collapse.
Photograph everything for your insurance claim.
Stay out of any room with a sagging or compromised ceiling.
When to call: Call a roofer once conditions are safe. Never climb onto a wet or storm-damaged roof yourself, and be wary of storm-chasers who show up uninvited.

sections.heading: Water heater leaking or failing
paragraphs: A leaking or failed water heater can flood a space quickly and, on gas models, occasionally involve a gas hazard.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Shut off the cold-water valve on top of the tank.
Turn off the power at the breaker, or set a gas unit's control to off.
If you smell gas near a gas heater, stop and treat it as a gas emergency instead.
Contain and mop up the water; photograph any damage.
When to call: Call a plumber for the repair or replacement. For a gas model with a gas smell, call the gas company or 911 first.

sections.heading: Power outage
paragraphs: Most outages are on the utility's side, but some start at your own panel — and the response differs.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Check whether neighbors are also dark (a utility outage) or just your home (a breaker or main problem).
Unplug sensitive electronics to protect them from a surge when power returns.
Keep the refrigerator and freezer closed to preserve food.
Use flashlights rather than candles to avoid a fire.
When to call: Report a utility outage to your power company. If only your home is out, or the panel is hot, scorched, or smells like burning, call a licensed electrician.
Do not: Only ever run a portable generator outdoors, well away from windows and doors — its exhaust is deadly indoors.

sections.heading: Locked out of your home
paragraphs: A lockout is stressful and urgent, but rarely dangerous — the main risk is damaging a door or lock by forcing it.

sections.heading: Do this right now:
paragraphs: Check other doors and ground-floor windows in case one is open.
Call a household member or trusted neighbor who has a key.
Avoid DIY entry tricks that can damage the lock, the door, or the frame.
Wait somewhere safe rather than leaving the property unsecured.
When to call: Call a licensed locksmith. Call 911 if someone is inside and in danger, or if a child or pet is locked inside during extreme heat or cold.

sections.heading: Emergency quick reference
paragraphs: When there's no time to read, this is the whole playbook in one table.

sections.heading: Get out first; gas at meter if safe
How to prepare before an emergency
paragraphs: The calmest emergencies are the ones you've prepared for. A little setup now turns panic into a checklist later.
Locate and label your shutoffs — Tag the main water valve, gas meter, and electrical panel, and make sure everyone in the home can find them.
Build a basic emergency kit — Flashlights and batteries, a fire extinguisher (ABC), a pipe wrench for the gas valve, towels, a first-aid kit, and phone chargers or a power bank.
Keep a vetted pro list ready — Have a trusted plumber, electrician, and HVAC pro lined up before you need them, so you're not searching mid-crisis.

Maintain to prevent — Most emergencies are preventable — servicing your HVAC, checking the roof, and watching for small leaks heads off the big ones. Our year-round maintenance checklist covers the routine.
Know your insurance — Understand what your homeowner's policy covers and how to file a claim, and keep photos and receipts organized.

sections.heading: Urgent, but it can wait
paragraphs: Not everything that feels alarming is an emergency. A single dripping faucet, one dead outlet on an otherwise healthy panel, a running toilet, or an appliance that's stopped working can all wait long enough for you to compare pros, read reviews, and book the right person at a fair price. Handle them promptly — a slow leak still wastes water and can grow — but you don't need to shut anything off in a hurry or pay emergency rates. The goal is to reserve emergency urgency for genuine emergencies, and treat the rest as the routine repairs they are.

It won't stop the pipe from bursting, but it makes the next ten minutes a great deal calmer.

sections.heading: Key takeaways
paragraphs: People first: for fire, gas, or danger, get out and call 911 before anything else.
Stop the source — shut off the water, gas, or power that controls the problem.
Learn where your shutoffs are and how to operate them before you ever need to.
Gas, live electrical, and structural hazards are never DIY — get clear and call a pro.
Contain the damage and photograph everything for your insurance claim.
Prepare a kit and a vetted pro list; maintenance prevents most emergencies.

faqs.question: What should I do first in a home emergency?
faqs.answer: Make sure everyone is safe first — if there's fire, gas, or danger, get out and call 911. Then stop the source by shutting off the water, gas, or electricity that controls the problem, contain the damage, and call a licensed pro for the system involved.

faqs.question: How do I shut off the water to my house?
faqs.answer: Find the main water valve where the line enters your home — near the meter, in a basement, garage, or an outside box — and turn it clockwise (or a lever a quarter-turn) until it stops. For a single fixture, use the smaller valve under the sink or behind the appliance.

faqs.question: What should I do if I smell gas?
faqs.answer: Leave the house immediately with everyone and your pets, and don't flip switches, use phones, or light anything inside — a spark can ignite gas. From outside, call 911 and your gas utility. Don't go back in until they confirm it's safe. Never try to repair a gas line yourself.

faqs.question: Is no heat considered an emergency?
faqs.answer: During a hard freeze, yes — a heating failure can freeze and burst pipes, and some heat sources create carbon-monoxide risk. Protect your pipes by letting faucets drip, use only safe supplemental heat, and call an HVAC pro. On a mild day, no heat is urgent but not a true emergency.

faqs.question: What should I do if my basement or home floods?
faqs.answer: Shut off the water at the main, and cut power to the affected area if water is near outlets or wiring — never touch electrical while standing in water. Move valuables, document the damage with photos, and call a licensed plumber and, for large floods, a water-damage restoration pro.

faqs.question: Who do I call for a home emergency — 911 or a contractor?
faqs.answer: Call 911 for anything life-threatening: fire, a gas leak, active sparks or smoke, or a medical emergency. For property emergencies without immediate danger to people — a burst pipe, sewage backup, or heating failure — shut off the affected system and call a licensed pro for that trade.

faqs.question: How can I prepare for a home emergency?
faqs.answer: Locate and label your water, gas, and electrical shutoffs; build a basic kit with flashlights, a fire extinguisher, and a wrench for the gas valve; keep a vetted plumber, electrician, and HVAC pro on hand; keep up with maintenance; and know what your insurance covers.

articles.title: Repair or Replace? A Homeowner's Guide
articles.subtitle: How to Decide When to Fix It and When to Replace It
articles.metaDescription: Repair or replace? Use the 50% rule, expected lifespans, and a simple framework to decide whether to fix or replace your HVAC, water heater, roof, and appliances.
articles.ctaTitle: Not sure? Get an honest diagnosis.
articles.ctaBody: Describe what's going on and TradeWorks connects you with vetted, performance-scored pros for a straight answer — with upfront pricing on repairs and free quotes to compare on replacements. Membership is free, you pay the pro directly with no markup, and you earn service credits.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: The quick rule: repair a system or appliance when it's well within its expected lifespan, the fix costs a fraction of a replacement, and it's the first major failure. Replace it when it's near or past that lifespan, the repair would cost more than about half the price of a new unit (the 50% rule), it keeps breaking, or a newer, efficient model would pay for itself in lower energy bills. The rest of this guide turns that rule into a decision you can make with confidence.

sections.heading: Why getting this decision right matters
paragraphs: Every homeowner eventually faces the same fork in the road: the air conditioner quits in July, the water heater starts leaking, or the refrigerator won't stay cold, and a technician asks whether you want to repair it or replace it. Get it wrong in one direction and you pour hundreds or thousands of dollars into a unit that fails again a month later. Get it wrong in the other and you scrap something with years of good service left.

The trap most people fall into is the sunk-cost trap — “I've already spent $300 on this thing, I might as well fix it again.” Money you've already spent is gone either way; the only question that matters is what gives you the best value from today forward. A simple framework, applied honestly, beats guessing or reacting to the pressure of a hot day and a persuasive quote.

It's worth naming the pressure these decisions usually come with. The AC dies on the hottest day, the water heater floods a closet, the refrigerator fails with a week of groceries inside — you're stressed, uncomfortable, and staring at a technician who's ready to sell. That's the worst state to make a four- or five-figure decision in. The whole point of a framework is that it lets you slow down for ten minutes, run the numbers, and reach the same call you'd make on a calm afternoon.

sections.heading: The repair-or-replace framework: seven questions
paragraphs: Run any broken or aging item through these seven questions. The more that point toward replacement, the clearer the call.
1. How old is it, relative to its expected lifespan? An item in the first half of its life usually deserves a repair; one near or past its lifespan is a replacement candidate.
2. Does the repair pass the 50% rule? If the fix costs more than roughly half the price of a comparable new unit, replacement is usually the better value.
3. How often has it broken? A first failure is normal wear; a third or fourth repair in a couple of years signals a unit that's wearing out.
4. What will a newer model cost to run? Efficiency has improved dramatically. A new HVAC system, water heater, or refrigerator can cut operating costs enough to offset part of its price over time.
5. Is there a safety or code issue? Cracked heat exchangers, recalled parts, outdated wiring, or refrigerants being phased out can tip the decision to replace regardless of age.
6. Are parts still available? For discontinued models, a needed part may be expensive, back-ordered, or simply unavailable — which forces a replacement anyway.
7. How long will you stay in the home? If you're moving soon, a targeted repair may make more sense; if you're staying for years, a replacement's savings and reliability have time to pay off.

sections.heading: The 50% rule (and the age-times-cost rule)
paragraphs: The single most useful shortcut is the 50% rule: if a repair costs more than about half the price of a new equivalent, replacing usually wins. It captures the idea that money spent on a dying unit rarely returns as much value as money spent on a new one with a full lifespan and warranty ahead of it.

sections.heading: Worked example
paragraphs: A repair on an 11-year-old central AC is quoted at $2,400. A comparable new system installed is about $6,000. The repair is 40% of replacement — under the 50% line — but the unit is past its typical lifespan and using an older refrigerant, so several other questions point to replacement. When age and the 50% rule disagree, weigh the other five questions.
A dishwasher repair is quoted at $320 against a $700 replacement — 46%, and the unit is only five years old. Here, repair is the clear, easy call.

A useful companion is the age-times-cost rule (sometimes called the $5,000 rule): multiply the appliance's age in years by the repair cost. If the result is more than about $5,000, lean toward replacement. A ten-year-old dryer with a $300 repair scores 3,000 — repair; a fourteen-year-old refrigerator with a $500 repair scores 7,000 — replace. Treat both rules as guides, not gospel; they're most powerful when they agree with the age and efficiency questions above.

sections.heading: Typical lifespans and repair-or-replace rules by system
paragraphs: Lifespans vary with use, climate, water quality, and maintenance, but these typical ranges anchor the age question. Use the last two columns as quick tie-breakers.

sections.heading: 15–20 yrs
paragraphs: Under ~10 yrs and the fix is well under half of new

sections.heading: 12+ yrs, older refrigerant, or repeated failures

Repair or replace, system by system
Heating and cooling (HVAC)
paragraphs: HVAC is usually the biggest-ticket decision, so the framework earns its keep here. A newer system under ten years old with a failed capacitor or motor is almost always worth repairing. But once a unit is past twelve to fifteen years, uses a phased-out refrigerant, or needs a compressor or heat exchanger, replacement usually wins — a modern high-efficiency system can meaningfully lower your energy bills, and you avoid a string of repairs on aging parts. A cracked heat exchanger is a safety issue that points to replacement regardless of the math. One more factor unique to HVAC: a replacement is also the moment to correct an undersized or oversized system and fix duct problems, which a repair simply can't do — so a new install can perform noticeably better, not merely newer.

sections.heading: Water heater
paragraphs: A tank water heater in its first several years with a bad thermostat or element is a straightforward repair. Once it's past about ten years, producing rusty water, or — most tellingly — leaking from the tank itself, replace it. A leaking tank can't be repaired, and a failure can flood the space around it. Tankless units last far longer, so most tankless repairs are worthwhile well into their second decade.

sections.heading: Roof
paragraphs: An isolated leak or a small section of damaged shingles on an otherwise healthy roof is a repair. Widespread damage, multiple leaks, sagging, or a roof past twenty-five years leans strongly toward replacement — patching a worn-out roof only delays the inevitable while water finds new ways in. After a storm, get a professional assessment before deciding, and be cautious of anyone knocking on your door promising a free new roof through your insurance.

sections.heading: Major kitchen and laundry appliances
paragraphs: For refrigerators, washers, dryers, dishwashers, and ranges, the 50% and age-times-cost rules do most of the work. Cheap, common fixes — a dryer belt, a dishwasher pump, an oven igniter — on a unit under about eight years old are worth doing. Sealed-system or compressor failures in a refrigerator, or a major motor or control-board failure in an older machine, usually cost enough that a new, more efficient model is the smarter buy. Factor in that newer appliances often use noticeably less energy and water. It also helps to separate the appliance from its accessories — a failed ice maker, a worn door gasket, or a clogged pump is a cheap, isolated fix even on an older refrigerator or washer, and shouldn't by itself push you toward replacing the whole unit.

sections.heading: Windows, doors, and the small stuff
paragraphs: Windows with a broken seal, foggy glass, persistent drafts, or rotting frames are candidates for replacement, especially if an efficiency upgrade is on your list; a single failed lock or balance, though, is a repair. For small items like garbage disposals and faucets, replacement is often as cheap as a serious repair and buys you a fresh warranty, so the calculus tips toward replacing more readily than it does for big systems.

sections.heading: Don't forget the hidden factors
paragraphs: The sticker price of a repair or a replacement isn't the whole story. A few less-obvious factors can change the decision.

Operating cost — A more efficient unit lowers your monthly bills. Over years, those savings can offset a meaningful share of a replacement's price — so a slightly pricier new model can be cheaper to own.

Rebates and tax credits — Utility rebates and tax incentives for high-efficiency HVAC, water heaters, and appliances may be available and can shift the math. Check current federal, state, and local programs, since they change.
Warranty and reliability — A new unit comes with a full warranty and years of expected trouble-free service; another repair on an old one comes with neither.
Downtime and disruption — There's a real cost to repeated breakdowns — spoiled food, cold showers, missed work waiting for a technician. Reliability has value beyond the invoice.
Resale — If you're selling soon, buyers notice aging systems; if you're staying, you get the full benefit of the upgrade.

sections.heading: When to lean repair vs. replace
paragraphs: Lean repair when: the item is in the first half of its life, the fix is well under half the cost of new, it's the first real failure, and parts are readily available.

Lean replace when: it's near or past its lifespan, the repair breaks the 50% rule, it keeps failing, a new model would pay you back in efficiency, or there's a safety, code, or parts-availability problem.
When the signals are mixed, get a second opinion and a written quote for both options before you decide — which is exactly where a trustworthy, vetted pro makes the difference.

sections.heading: Common repair-or-replace mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: A few predictable mistakes trip up even careful homeowners. Knowing them in advance is half the battle.
Chasing the cheapest quote — the lowest repair price can hide missing scope or a fix that won't last. Compare what each pro is actually doing, not just the number at the bottom.
Ignoring efficiency — judging on sticker price alone misses the operating-cost savings that can make a new, efficient unit cheaper to own over its life.
Falling for the sunk-cost trap — what you've already spent on past repairs has no bearing on today's decision. Only future value counts.
Replacing too early — a serviceable unit with one affordable failure doesn't need to be scrapped. The framework guards against over-buying as much as under-buying.
Repairing too long — the flip side: a third or fourth repair on an aging unit is usually good money chasing bad.
DIY on the wrong systems — gas, electrical, and roofing work carries real risk and often needs a permit. Those repairs belong to a licensed pro whichever way the decision falls.

faqs.question: What is the 50% rule for repair or replace?
faqs.answer: If a repair costs more than about half the price of a comparable new unit, replacement is usually the better value. It's a rule of thumb — weigh it alongside the item's age, how often it's failed, and how efficient a new model would be.

faqs.question: Should I repair or replace my air conditioner?
faqs.answer: Repair a unit under about ten years old with an affordable fix. Replace one that's past twelve to fifteen years, uses a phased-out refrigerant, needs a compressor, or keeps breaking — a new high-efficiency system often lowers your energy bills enough to help offset the cost.

faqs.question: How do I know if an appliance is worth fixing?
faqs.answer: Apply the 50% rule and the age-times-cost rule (age in years times repair cost; over about $5,000 leans replace), and consider the appliance's typical lifespan. Cheap, common fixes on a newer unit are worth it; major failures on an older one usually aren't.

faqs.question: When should I replace my water heater instead of repairing it?
faqs.answer: Replace a tank water heater once it's past about ten years, producing rusty water, or leaking from the tank itself — a leaking tank can't be repaired and can flood the area. A newer unit with a bad element or thermostat is a simple repair.

faqs.question: Does replacing an old system really save money?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Efficiency has improved a lot, so a new HVAC system, water heater, or refrigerator can cost noticeably less to run. Over several years those savings can offset a meaningful share of the replacement price, and current rebates or tax credits may help further.

faqs.question: How long do major home systems last?
faqs.answer: Typical ranges: central AC and furnaces about 15–20 years, heat pumps 12–15, tank water heaters 8–12 (tankless 15–20), asphalt roofs 20–30, refrigerators 10–15, and most other major appliances roughly 10–13 years. Use and maintenance shift these up or down.

faqs.question: Are there rebates for replacing old appliances or HVAC?
faqs.answer: There may be. Utilities and governments often offer rebates or tax credits for high-efficiency HVAC, water heaters, and appliances, but programs change frequently, so check current federal, state, local, and utility offers before you buy.

articles.subtitle: Undo Winter, Get Ready for Summer — Area by Area

articles.ctaTitle: Get spring done — book a vetted pro

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Spring home maintenance is about undoing winter's wear and getting ready for summer heat. The essentials: service the air conditioner before the first hot spell, clean the gutters and inspect the roof for winter damage, check outdoor faucets and sprinklers for freeze damage, wash and reseal exterior surfaces, and refresh your safety devices. Start outside, where winter did the most damage, then work your way in.

sections.heading: Why spring maintenance matters
paragraphs: Winter is hard on a house. Freeze-and-thaw cycles work at roofing and masonry, ice and wind loosen shingles and clog gutters, and months of closed-up cold leave moisture and stale air behind. Spring is the reset — the season to find and fix what winter left, and to get ahead of the two things summer brings: heat and, in many areas, storms.

The payoff is the same as with all maintenance: problems are cheap to fix when they're small. A single lifted shingle, a hairline crack in a hose bib, or a condenser buried in leaves costs little to address now and a great deal more if you wait until a summer storm, a burst pipe, or a heat-wave breakdown forces the issue. Work through the checklist below in whatever order suits you, but if you do nothing else, get your air conditioner serviced before you need it.

Spring also has a psychological advantage: it's the natural moment to take stock. After months of hunkering down, walking the property with fresh eyes turns a vague sense that you should check on a few things into a concrete plan. Doing it once, thoroughly, in spring means you're not scrambling to react all summer. You've already found the problems on your own schedule, when they're small and cheap, instead of on the weather's schedule, when they're not.

sections.heading: The spring maintenance checklist, area by area
paragraphs: Here's the full walkthrough, grouped by area so you can tackle it a section at a time. Check off what applies to your home, and hand off the jobs that involve heights, specialized tools, or licensed trades.

paragraphs: Winter is toughest on the roof, so start here — and catch damage before spring rains find it. Everything downstream of a roof problem, from the walls to the ceilings to the insulation, costs more to fix than the roof itself, so this is time well spent.
Inspect the roof from the ground for lifted, cracked, or missing shingles

sections.heading: Check the flashing around chimneys, skylights, and vents
Clean gutters and downspouts of leaves and winter debris
Confirm downspouts direct water well away from the foundation
paragraphs: Look in the attic for water stains or daylight that signal a leak
Book a pro for: a roof inspection or repair, and gutter cleaning on a multi-story home

sections.heading: Exterior and siding
paragraphs: A slow walk around the outside of your home reveals most of what winter left behind.

sections.heading: Wash siding and remove any mildew or grime
paragraphs: Check paint and caulk around trim, windows, and doors, and touch up as needed

sections.heading: Inspect the foundation and exterior walls for new cracks
Clean and inspect walkways, steps, and the driveway
Check outdoor lighting and replace bulbs

sections.heading: Cooling and HVAC
paragraphs: The single most important spring task is getting your air conditioner ready before the first heat wave. A spring tune-up is far cheaper than an emergency call in July.

sections.heading: Schedule a professional AC tune-up early, before the rush
Replace the HVAC filter

sections.heading: Windows and doors

paragraphs: Spring is prime time to get your landscape healthy and your drainage working before summer. Overgrown branches near the house or power lines are also a storm liability, so this doubles as early storm prep.

sections.heading: Safety and systems
paragraphs: A few minutes on your home's safety devices is the highest-return task on this entire list. It costs nothing and takes minutes, yet it is the difference that matters most in a real emergency.

paragraphs: Finish inside, where winter moisture and stale air need attention.
Check the attic and basement or crawl space for moisture, leaks, or pests

sections.heading: Deep-clean and replace interior air filters
Find and seal any remaining drafts
Inspect and refresh caulking in bathrooms and the kitchen
paragraphs: Book a pro for: an attic or moisture inspection and pest control
A closer look at the big three: roof, AC, and water intrusion
Three spring items carry more weight than the rest, because getting them wrong is where the big, expensive failures come from. They are worth a little extra attention.

sections.heading: The roof
paragraphs: Your roof took the brunt of winter. Even without a leak yet, freeze-and-thaw cycles and wind can loosen shingles and lift flashing, creating the gaps that spring rain then exploits. A ground-level inspection catches the obvious problems; an attic check for stains or daylight catches the ones you cannot see from below. If your roof is older, weathered a rough winter, or shows any of these signs, get a professional assessment before the rainy season, because a small repair now is a fraction of the cost of the water damage a neglected gap causes.

sections.heading: The air conditioner
paragraphs: An air conditioner that sat idle all winter can hide a failing capacitor, low refrigerant, or a clogged condensate line that only reveals itself under load. Testing and servicing it in spring, on a mild day and before the season peak, means any problem surfaces with time and options rather than on the hottest afternoon of the year when every HVAC company is booked solid. It is the clearest example of the whole spring principle: fix it on your schedule, not the weather's.

sections.heading: Points where water can get in
paragraphs: Most expensive home damage traces back to water finding a way in, so spring is the time to close those paths. Reseal cracked caulk around windows and doors, patch foundation cracks, confirm the ground slopes away from the house, make sure gutters and downspouts carry water well clear of the foundation, and test the sump pump. None of these tasks is glamorous, and all of them are cheap next to the mold, rot, and structural repair that water intrusion eventually causes.

sections.heading: Spring priorities: do these first
paragraphs: If your time is limited, these are the tasks with the biggest payoff — the ones that prevent the most expensive or dangerous problems later in the year.
1. Service the air conditioner before the first hot spell.
2. Inspect the roof and clean the gutters before spring rains.
3. Check every point where water could get in — flashing, caulk, foundation, and grading.
4. Test and refresh smoke and carbon-monoxide detectors.
5. Inspect outdoor plumbing and the sump pump before you need them.

sections.heading: Early, mid, and late spring
paragraphs: Spreading these tasks across the season keeps any one weekend from becoming overwhelming.
Early spring — assess the winter damage while it's fresh: inspect the roof, clean the gutters, walk the exterior and foundation, and check outdoor plumbing as the last freeze passes.
Mid spring — get ahead of summer: schedule the AC tune-up, wash and reseal exterior surfaces and the deck, start up irrigation, and begin yard and landscaping work.
Late spring — finish the summer prep: confirm the AC is running well, stay ahead of pests, seal up the last gaps, and get outdoor living spaces ready for the season.

sections.heading: Don't overlook the hidden spaces
paragraphs: The easiest spring tasks to skip are the ones you cannot see, namely the attic, the basement, and the crawl space, which is exactly why they deserve a look, since winter moisture, roof leaks, and pests all tend to show up here first. Head into the attic and check for water stains, damp insulation, daylight through the roof, and any sign that animals moved in for the winter. Check the basement or crawl space for dampness, a musty smell, chalky efflorescence on the walls, or standing water, all of which point to a drainage or sealing problem worth fixing before summer humidity makes it worse. While you are there, note whether the insulation is adequate and dry, since it affects both your cooling bills and your home's resistance to moisture. Ten minutes in these spaces can surface a problem months before it would announce itself in your living room.

sections.heading: What to DIY and when to call a pro
paragraphs: Plenty of spring maintenance is satisfying weekend work. The line to respect, as always, is height, specialized equipment, and licensed trades.

Adjust for your climate
paragraphs: Spring looks different depending on where you live, so do the tasks that fit your home. In areas with hard winters, focus on freeze-and-thaw damage — the roof, masonry, and outdoor pipes — as the last frost passes. In hot, humid regions, prioritize the AC tune-up and pest prevention, since summer arrives fast. In storm-prone areas, fold storm preparation into your spring routine: secure loose exterior items, trim overhanging branches, and confirm your drainage and sump pump are ready. The checklist is the menu; your climate decides the order. Timing shifts too: the last frost that makes it safe to start up outdoor plumbing might come in February in one place and May in another, so let your local conditions, not the calendar page, tell you when to begin.
